findings.title: identity.verified is audited AFTER the VERIFIED record is committed — fail-closed guarantee is violated on the trust-granting action
findings.scenario: In verify() the record is persisted (self._store.put(record)) and remembered in the registry, THEN _announce() calls auditor.record('identity.verified', ...). identity.verified is declared critical (auditable_actions.py) and AUDIT_FAIL_CLOSED defaults True, so when the audit log is down auditor.record raises AuditUnavailable AFTER the record is already stored as verdict=VERIFIED. The caller receives a 503 (AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE) implying nothing happened, but status()/latest() now return VERIFIED and the downstream welcome-gift/account-open can already be issued off it. The fail-closed control it exists for (an unprovable grant must not proceed) is defeated: the grant proceeded and is unprovable. On the caller's retry a brand-new record is created — a second provider call (real money) and a second registry.remember() increment for the same identity.
findings.evidence:
outcome = await self._ask(...)
        self._apply(record, outcome, now)
        await self._store.put(record)
        await self._announce(record, outcome)   # <- auditor.record('identity.verified') runs here, can raise after commit
findings.recommendation: Audit write-ahead for the critical grant (record the intent before _store.put, as operator.py does for secret_set), or make the put+audit atomic with rollback on AuditUnavailable. Never commit a verdict the critical audit could still refuse.
findings.fix: The critical identity.verified audit is now WRITTEN AHEAD of the put via a new _commit(): for a VERIFIED verdict the audit is recorded first, so a down/fail-closed audit log (AUDIT_FAIL_CLOSED) raises AuditUnavailable BEFORE the verdict is stored — the caller's 503 now truthfully means nothing happened, and status()/latest() do not return a VERIFIED downstream can act on. verify() and resolve() both route through _commit. Refusals/errors stay stored-then-audited non-critically (a down log must not block a refusal). Regression tests in tests/unit/test_verification.py.

findings.title: Runtime config changes bypass the boot guard — VERIFY_PROVIDERS can be repointed to the null verifier / an invalid provider at runtime
findings.scenario: runtime_config.py's own docstring promises 'THE BOOT GUARD'S RULES APPLY AT RUNTIME TOO' and RuntimeConfig.set() only re-runs the guard when self._validate is set. But _runtime_config() in operator.py constructs RuntimeConfig(datastore, Settings, policy=RUNTIME_POLICY) with NO validate= argument (also the app.state one in main.py). VERIFY_PROVIDERS is the one settable key. An operator can PUT /operator/config VERIFY_PROVIDERS=individual=null (or a provider with no url / no verdict_path) — values assert_verify_config_ok() refuses at boot in production — and it is accepted, coerced to str, stored, and applied by the pool. Every 'individual' check then returns ERROR (or, with a mis-mapped verdict, risks fail-open), while the panel shows the change succeeded and the audit log records it. The guard that protects the whole point of the service is silently not wired at the runtime edge.
findings.evidence: return RuntimeConfig(request.app.state.container.datastore, Settings, policy=RUNTIME_POLICY)   # validate= omitted -> self._validate is None -> set() skips assert_verify_config_ok
findings.recommendation: Pass a validate callback into every RuntimeConfig construction that re-runs the relevant boot guards (at minimum assert_verify_config_ok for VERIFY_PROVIDERS), so a runtime override is refused exactly as a boot value would be.
findings.fix: Every RuntimeConfig construction (main.py app.state + operator.py fallback) now passes validate=settings.runtime_validate, a new Settings method that re-runs assert_verify_config_ok() against the candidate value (model_copy with the new VERIFY_PROVIDERS). RuntimeConfig.set() converts a boot-guard ValueError into RuntimeConfigError so the panel gets a 400-with-reason. A null/urlless provider that production refuses at boot is now refused at runtime too. Regression test tests/integration/test_operator_surface.py::test_runtime_override_faces_the_production_boot_guard.

findings.title: resolve() has no compare-and-set — concurrent duplicate provider callbacks double-settle, double-audit, and corrupt the once-per-identity count
findings.scenario: decide() was hardened to cas_put() precisely because a read-check-write on a PENDING record races. resolve() still does the old unsafe pattern: get(), check verdict==PENDING, _apply(), plain store.put(), _announce(). Providers retry callbacks, so two retried 'verified' callbacks for one id can both read PENDING, both pass the check, both put and both _announce. Result: two 'identity.verified' audit rows for one grant and, worse, registry.remember() runs twice for the same claim_ref so times becomes 2 on a single genuine verification — the anti-abuse counter onboarding relies on ('has this identity collected the grant') is corrupted. The docstring claims IDEMPOTENT but idempotence here is not concurrency-safe.
findings.evidence:
if record.verdict != PENDING:
            return record
        ...
        self._apply(record, outcome, now)
        record.provider_state = {}
        await self._store.put(record)          # not cas_put; no version guard
        await self._announce(record, outcome)
findings.recommendation: Settle via store.cas_put() and, on a lost race, refetch and return the now-settled record unchanged — the same atomic seam decide() already uses.
findings.fix: resolve() now settles via cas_put with refetch-on-conflict in a bounded loop (was get→check→plain put): two retried callbacks can no longer both read PENDING and both write; the loser refetches and returns the settled record. Regression test with an interleaving store.

findings.title: review.decided is audited AFTER cas_put commits the decision — same fail-closed-after-commit defect as verify()
findings.scenario: decide() commits the VERIFIED/REFUSED verdict with cas_put() and breaks out of the loop, THEN calls auditor.record('review.decided', ...). review.decided is declared critical. If the audit log is down, auditor.record raises AuditUnavailable after the manual approval — the highest-privilege operation in the service — is already persisted. The reviewer gets a 503 as though the decision was refused, but the claim is already VERIFIED and cannot be re-decided (the settled-check now refuses a retry with 'already verified'). So a human grant of trust becomes permanent AND unprovable, which is exactly the condition critical/fail-closed exists to prevent.
findings.recommendation: Write-ahead the review.decided audit (or make commit+audit atomic with rollback). A settled-but-unaudited critical decision is the worst outcome.
findings.fix: decide() write-ahead-audits review.decided BEFORE the final cas_put (was after commit); a down critical audit log refuses the decision before it persists. The committed decision is always the one audited immediately before it.

findings.title: status() never lapses a PENDING record on read — a lapsed async prompt reports 'pending' forever until a sweep runs, contradicting 'expiry evaluated on read'
findings.scenario: The file's rule #2 and is_trusted() compute VERIFIED expiry on read so a stale verdict is never trusted before a sweeper runs. But status() only downgrades VERIFIED->EXPIRED; for a PENDING record whose pending_until has already passed it returns verdict='pending', trusted=False. If the sweep CronJob has not run and no callback arrives, a user polling /status sees 'pending' indefinitely for a prompt that has actually lapsed. is_trusted() also returns False for PENDING but never reflects the lapse in the reported verdict. The on-read lapse guarantee the service advertises does not cover the pending state — only the verified state.
findings.recommendation: In status()/is_trusted(), when verdict==PENDING and pending_until and now>=pending_until, report EXPIRED — evaluate the lapse on read exactly as expiry is.
findings.fix: status() now downgrades a PENDING record whose pending_until has passed to EXPIRED on READ, exactly as VERIFIED expiry is evaluated — a lapsed prompt no longer reports 'pending' forever when the sweep hasn't run. Regression test added.

findings.title: sweep_pending() uses store.put() not cas_put() — it can clobber a concurrent resolve()/decide() that just settled the record
findings.scenario: sweep_pending() reads the pending-before set, then for each record sets verdict=EXPIRED and calls store.put() with no version check. A provider callback (resolve) or a reviewer (decide) can settle a record to VERIFIED/REFUSED between the sweep's find() and its put(); the sweep's unconditional put() then overwrites that real decision with EXPIRED. Because put() serializes the record's current version unchanged, it silently wins the write with no CAS. A legitimately verified identity can be flipped to EXPIRED by a racing sweep near the pending_until boundary.
findings.evidence:
for record in await self._store.pending_before(now, limit=limit):
            record.verdict = EXPIRED
            record.updated_at = now
            await self._store.put(record)          # no version guard, unlike decide()
findings.recommendation: Sweep with cas_put() and skip (do not retry into EXPIRED) any record whose verdict is no longer PENDING on refetch.
findings.fix: sweep_pending() lapses via cas_put with a refetch+status recheck: a provider callback/reviewer settling a record between find() and the write is preserved (the sweep skips a no-longer-PENDING row) instead of being clobbered with EXPIRED.

findings.title: resolve() accepts any verified=true for a PENDING id with no provider-correlation/nonce check — an internal caller (or a bug) can approve any pending verification by id
findings.scenario: PENDING records store provider_state (the correlation token from the provider callback), but resolve() ignores it entirely: it takes verification_id + verified and settles. The verification_id is returned to the end user in the submit_claim response (record.public() includes id). The only gate on POST /internal/verification/resolve is the shared internal token — there is no verification that the caller is the provider that owns this pending check, and no match of body.reference against the stored provider_state correlation token. Any component holding the internal token, or a confused-deputy bug, can turn any user's pending identity check into VERIFIED by replaying its id with verified=true.
findings.evidence:
outcome = vp.Outcome(status=vp.VERIFIED if verified else vp.REFUSED,
                             provider=record.evidence.get("provider", ""),
                             reference=reference, detail=detail)
        self._apply(record, outcome, now)   # provider_state / correlation token never checked
findings.recommendation: Require and verify the provider correlation token stored in provider_state against the callback before settling, so a resolve must prove it came from the provider that owns the pending prompt.
findings.fix: resolve() now verifies the callback's reference against the provider correlation token captured in provider_state (the pending outcome's reference); a mismatch raises CorrelationMismatch → 403. Records with no captured correlation are unchanged (backward compatible). Regression test added.

findings.title: Erasure rewrites records with non-atomic store.put(), racing decide()/resolve() cas writes and losing either side
findings.scenario: VerificationErasure.erase() loads the subject's records and for each sets subject='' , provider_state={} and calls store.put() with no version guard. If a reviewer decides or a provider callback resolves the same record concurrently (both use cas_put), the erasure put() can overwrite a just-committed verdict (or vice versa), producing a record whose subject link is severed but whose provider_state/verdict is inconsistent with the decision. Erasure is irreversible, so a lost write here is unrecoverable.
findings.recommendation: Use cas_put with refetch-on-conflict for the erasure rewrite, or take the record through the same optimistic-lock path the decision writes use.
findings.fix: VerificationErasure.erase() severs the subject link with cas_put+refetch, re-applying subject=''/provider_state={} onto the freshest row, so a concurrent decide()/resolve() verdict is preserved and the link always goes. Regression test added.

findings.title: submit_claim relies on the default rate class (100 req / 60 s) — the provider-cost + enumeration endpoint has no strict default budget out of the box
findings.scenario: submit_claim's docstring says it is rate-limited because 'verification calls cost money at the provider, and an unthrottled endpoint is both a bill and an enumeration oracle.' But with RATELIMIT_ROUTES empty (the default) the route gets the default class RATELIMIT_MAX=100 per RATELIMIT_WINDOW_SECONDS=60 per subject. 100 provider-billed identity checks per minute per authenticated subject is neither a brute-force nor a cost defense; the tight budget the endpoint needs exists only if an operator remembers to add a route class. A shipped-secure default should classify the claims-submit path strictly.
findings.evidence:
RATELIMIT_MAX: int = 100
    RATELIMIT_WINDOW_SECONDS: int = 60
    RATELIMIT_ROUTES: str = ""                  # JSON: [...]  (empty by default)
findings.recommendation: Ship a default RATELIMIT_ROUTES entry (or a dedicated class) for /api/v1/verification/claims with a low limit/window, so the money+enumeration endpoint is throttled without operator action.

findings.title: HttpVerifier egress is not checked against EGRESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS — the declared SSRF allowlist (CWE-918) is unenforced on the provider call
findings.scenario: config.py declares EGRESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS / egress_allowed_hosts (CWE-918 SSRF allowlist) and the CWE guard exists, but HttpVerifier._fetch() calls urllib.request.urlopen(url) directly on the profile url with no host allowlist check. The url is config-supplied (lower risk than a request-supplied one), and an operator can now repoint VERIFY_PROVIDERS at runtime; combined with a redirect-following urlopen, a mis- or maliciously-configured profile url can reach internal metadata endpoints. The declared control simply does not cover this egress path.
findings.recommendation: Validate the profile url host against settings.egress_allowed_hosts before the call (and disable redirects), so provider egress is bound by the same allowlist the platform declares.

findings.title: registry.remember() failure is swallowed with bare 'except: pass' — the anti-abuse key can be silently missing on a VERIFIED identity
findings.scenario: _announce() wraps registry.remember() in try/except: pass 'so a registry write failing must not un-verify a genuine identity'. But the comment claims 'the grant side refuses rather than assuming' — nothing here records or counts the gap. If the identity_seen write fails, the identity is VERIFIED but never recorded as seen, so onboarding's once-per-identity check reads first_seen=True on a repeat and the welcome grant can be collected again — the exact fraud the registry exists to stop — with no telemetry, log, or audit trail of the miss.
findings.recommendation: Emit a telemetry event / warning log on the remember() failure (as the auditor does for gaps), so a missing anti-abuse key is observable rather than silent.

findings.title: status() echoes evidence.detail (raw provider refusal/error text) back to the end user as 'reason'
findings.scenario: status() returns reason=record.evidence.get('detail',''). For an HTTP verifier error/refusal, detail is provider-derived text such as 'provider returned HTTP 500', 'provider answered \'MISMATCH\'', or 'verifier raised: <exception>' (set in _ask). This is returned verbatim on a user-facing GET /status, potentially leaking provider internals, exception fragments, or backend hints — a milder cousin of the CWE-209 stripping the global error handler applies everywhere else.
findings.evidence: "reason": record.evidence.get("detail", "")
findings.recommendation: Return a small, mapped set of user-safe reason codes to the user tier; keep the raw provider detail in evidence for the audit/review surfaces only.

findings.title: Two-eyes applies only to approvals — a single reviewer can unilaterally REFUSE under a two-eyes policy
findings.scenario: The two-eyes accumulation branch is guarded by 'if approve and self._two_eyes'. A refusal (approve=False) skips it entirely and settles the verification to REFUSED on the first reviewer, even when VERIFY_TWO_EYES is on. In a regulated onboarding where the platform decided one person must not grant trust alone, one person can still DENY trust alone — a denial is also a consequential, appealable decision, and the control is silently one-sided. This branch is untested (test_two_eyes only exercises approvals).
findings.evidence:
if approve and self._two_eyes:
                ...
            record.evidence = Evidence(...)
            record.verdict = VERIFIED if approve else REFUSED   # single-reviewer refuse settles immediately
findings.recommendation: Decide and document whether two-eyes governs refusals too; if it should, apply the same two-reviewer tally to the refuse path, and add a test for single-reviewer-refuse-under-two-eyes.

findings.title: READYZ_TIMEOUT_SECONDS is read via getattr but never declared in Settings — the readiness timeout is unconfigurable despite the code implying it is
findings.scenario: readyz() does getattr(get_settings(), 'READYZ_TIMEOUT_SECONDS', _DEFAULT_READYZ_TIMEOUT). No READYZ_TIMEOUT_SECONDS field exists on the Settings class (config.py), so the getattr always falls through to the hardcoded 5.0 and setting the env var has no effect. An operator tuning the readiness timeout for a slow dependency (the very case the concurrent-probe comment describes) silently changes nothing.
findings.evidence: timeout = getattr(get_settings(), "READYZ_TIMEOUT_SECONDS", _DEFAULT_READYZ_TIMEOUT)
findings.recommendation: Declare READYZ_TIMEOUT_SECONDS on Settings (or drop the getattr and document the fixed value); a knob referenced in code but absent from config is a false promise.

findings.title: A PENDING (async) verification is never audited — an initiated identity check that awaits a phone prompt leaves no audit event
findings.scenario: _announce() audits only VERIFIED / REFUSED / ERROR. When a provider answers PENDING (Nafath-style prompt pushed to a phone), no auditor.record is emitted at all. The initiation of an identity check — who asked, for which claim, against which provider — is exactly the fraud-monitoring signal (PCI-DSS 10.2 / NIST AU-2 the file cites for refusals), yet a pending check that later lapses via the sweep produces zero audit trail of ever having been attempted.
findings.recommendation: Emit a non-critical 'identity.check_pending' (declared) audit event when a check is initiated as PENDING, so an attempt is witnessed even if it later lapses.

findings.title: Template probe routes /api/v1/whoami and /api/v1/admin/ping ship in a production service
findings.scenario: The v1 router still carries the _template's example routes: /whoami (echoes the caller's subject/caps/tenant) and /admin/ping (requires an 'admin' cap that this service never issues — its capability set is platform.*/verification.*). They are declared in the manifest too. whoami expands the authenticated surface with a caller-info reflector that no business flow needs, and admin/ping is dead (permanently 403) — both are template leftovers the header comment even flags as 'EXAMPLES — replace'.
findings.recommendation: Remove the template probe routes (and their manifest entries) or gate them behind a real capability; do not ship example endpoints in a trust-granting service.

findings.title: No tests cover the concurrency races, the pending-lapse-on-read gap, the single-reviewer-refuse branch, or audit-after-commit — the bugs are masked
findings.scenario: test_verification.py tests VERIFIED expiry-on-read and sequential resolve idempotency, but there is no test for: (a) concurrent duplicate resolve() callbacks (finding 003 — remember() double-increment / double audit); (b) a PENDING record reporting EXPIRED on status() after pending_until (finding 005 — the existing lapse test only calls resolve(), never status()); (c) a single reviewer refusing under two_eyes=True (finding 013); (d) verify()/decide() behaviour when the critical audit fails (findings 001/004). test_the_registry_answers_first_seen_exactly_once is sequential and never exercises the CAS race the remember() docstring claims to fix. A test that writes and reads through the same store measures the store, not the invariant.
findings.evidence:
def test_a_prompt_nobody_answers_lapses_rather_than_approving():
        ...
        late = run(svc.resolve(rec.id, verified=True))
        assert late.verdict == EXPIRED     # only via resolve(); status() on a lapsed pending is never asserted
findings.recommendation: Add concurrent-callback, status()-on-lapsed-pending, single-reviewer-refuse-under-two-eyes, and audit-unavailable-during-verify/decide tests so these invariants are actually measured.

findings.title: Operator secret/config routes accept an arbitrary tenant parameter with no per-tenant scope check
findings.scenario: list_secrets/set_secret/clear_secret and the config routes take tenant from the query/body and pass it straight to SecretStore/RuntimeConfig, gated only by require_capability('platform.secrets'/'platform.config'). A holder of platform.secrets whose own principal.tenant is A can read hints for, set, or clear credentials of any other tenant B by passing tenant=B; _actor() pseudonymises under the caller's own tenant, so the audit row does not even reflect the affected tenant. If platform.* is intended as a cross-tenant platform-admin capability this is by design, but nothing in this module documents or enforces that boundary, so a mis-scoped platform.secrets grant becomes fleet-wide credential access.
findings.evidence:
async def set_secret(request: Request, body: SecretIn, principal: Principal = Depends(require_user)) -> dict:
    ...
    info = await _secret_store(request).set(tenant=body.tenant, name=body.name, value=body.value, ...)   # body.tenant unvalidated against principal
findings.recommendation: Either assert the operation targets the caller's own tenant (unless a distinct platform-wide capability is held), or explicitly document platform.secrets/platform.config as cross-tenant and audit under the affected tenant.

findings.title: GET /claims (for_subject) is capped at 100 with no pagination — a subject with more claims silently sees only the newest 100
findings.scenario: my_claims() -> store.for_subject(tenant, subject) uses the default limit=100 and returns no cursor. A subject who has re-verified many times (each verify() creates a new row) sees only the 100 newest verdicts with no indication the list is truncated, so an older still-relevant verdict can silently disappear from 'every verdict about me'.
findings.evidence:
async def for_subject(self, tenant: str, subject: str, limit: int = 100) -> list[Verification]:
        rows, _ = await self._store.find(..., limit=limit, sort=("created_at", "desc"))
findings.recommendation: Return the find() cursor and expose pagination, or at least a 'truncated' flag, on GET /claims.

findings.title: Review queue limit is a hardcoded 100 (not config) and silently truncates
findings.scenario: queue() -> pending_reviews(tenant, limit=100) hardcodes 100 with no config knob and no truncation signal. Oldest-first means a backlog over 100 hides the newest pending items from the queue with no operator-visible indication, and the ceiling cannot be tuned without a code change.
findings.evidence:
async def queue(self, tenant: str, limit: int = 100) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
        rows = await self._store.pending_reviews(tenant, limit=limit)
findings.recommendation: Make the queue limit configurable and/or expose pagination + a truncated indicator.

findings.title: SecretStore.list_info caps at 200 rows — operator credentials beyond 200 are invisible in the panel listing
findings.scenario: list_info() -> find(_COLL, {'tenant': tenant}, limit=200, sort=('name','asc')). A deployment with more than 200 operator-managed credentials for a tenant would silently omit the rest from GET /operator/secrets, so an operator could believe a credential is unset (and re-create/overwrite it) when it merely fell past the listing cap.
findings.evidence: rows, _ = await self._s.find(_COLL, {"tenant": tenant}, limit=200, sort=("name", "asc"))
findings.recommendation: Paginate list_info or raise the cap to a real ceiling with a truncation indicator.

findings.title: VerifierPool resolves ALL provider credentials (datastore get + scrypt-decrypt) on every cache miss, even for a single-provider check
findings.scenario: _tokens() resolves a credential for every name in verify_secrets.values() on each cache rebuild, regardless of which claim type is being checked. With several providers configured, one expired-TTL check triggers a datastore read + AES/scrypt-backed decrypt for every provider credential, not just the one needed. The cache TTL bounds the frequency, but a low PROVIDER_REFRESH_SECONDS (required to stay under the rotation window) multiplies this fan-out.
findings.evidence:
return {name: await self._credential(tenant, name)
                for name in self._s.verify_secrets.values()}
findings.recommendation: Resolve credentials lazily per provider actually used, or cache per-credential with its own TTL, so an unrelated provider's decrypt is not on the rebuild path.

findings.title: Erasure swallows object-store delete failures silently — a stranded ID-card image leaves no signal
findings.scenario: When deleting an uploaded document (a photo of an ID card — the person's data in the plainest sense) the delete is wrapped in try/except: pass with only a comment that 'a stranded blob is swept by retention.' If the object store delete fails, the document count is not incremented but nothing is logged or counted, so a DSAR can report success while a real ID-card image remains in the object store, and no telemetry surfaces the failed erasure of personal data.
findings.recommendation: Emit a telemetry event / warning on the failed document delete and reflect it in the erasure ack so an incomplete erasure is observable.

findings.title: _json_any_map returns {} on malformed JSON — a mistyped INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON silently disables the internal route allow-list (default-open)
findings.scenario: _json_any_map() catches ValueError/TypeError and returns {} for empty OR malformed input. INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON is parsed through it (via _build_policy); a syntax error in the policy JSON yields an empty policy, which InternalRoutePolicy treats as default-open (any authenticated caller may reach every /internal route). A per-route caller allow-list an operator believed they had configured is silently absent, with no boot failure. The same silent-{} behaviour also drops a malformed RATELIMIT/caller-keys map.
findings.recommendation: Fail boot on malformed (non-empty) JSON for security-relevant maps like INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON rather than degrading to an empty, default-open policy.
